What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached? Interstellar travel, an endeavor steeped in both scientific curiosity and the realm of science fiction, presents a formidable challenge to our current technological capabilities. The very distances involved are so vast that conventional propulsion methods, such as chemical rockets, become utterly impractical. Even the most efficient chemical rockets would take tens of thousands of years to reach even the nearest star. To even begin to contemplate interstellar travel, we have to delve into the realm of theoretical propulsion systems. Among the most promising, at least in theory, are those based on the principles of nuclear fusion. Fusion, the process that powers the sun, could, theoretically, be harnessed to generate tremendous thrust and, more importantly, deliver a high exhaust velocity. This would allow for a significant fraction of the speed of light to be achieved. Other theoretical concepts, worthy of mention, include antimatter-based propulsion, although the technical hurdles involved in producing and storing antimatter are currently gargantuan. Then there's the concept of the Bussard ramjet, a theoretical fusion rocket that utilizes the interstellar medium itself as fuel, effectively scooping up hydrogen as it travels. However, this concept, as elegant as it appears, requires an extremely high density of interstellar material, and its actual efficiency can be questioned. Similarly, there are propulsion concepts that rely upon manipulating spacetime itself. Yet, these concepts are even more speculative than fusion-based propulsion, and their feasibility remains, to put it mildly, uncertain. As for what percentage of the speed of light we could conceivably attain, the answer depends on which technology gains traction. Fusion-powered rockets could realistically reach a substantial, albeit not quite relativistic, fraction of the speed of light. The theoretical limits are essentially imposed by the fundamental laws of physics and the practical constraints of engineering. Antimatter propulsion, if feasible, could, in principle, reach a far greater fraction of the speed of light, possibly close to it. But we are speaking of hypothetical scenarios, fraught with immense challenges. The journey to the stars, as a result, remains an aspiration, a testament to our intellectual curiosity and our unyielding desire to explore the vast cosmic expanse. In the meantime, let’s strive to advance the technologies that will make interstellar travel a tangible prospect, rather than a dream. I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed? Let's consider that. If the observer were to look back at the cosmos as he approached the black hole's event horizon, he would see something quite strange. The cosmos, the entire vast span of spacetime, would appear to compress, time dilation would be extreme. The observer could theoretically see the entire future of the universe, compressed into a final flash of light, before being irrevocably swallowed. But what about that observer? What happens "when" he crosses the event horizon? This is where things get, to put it mildly, complicated. Within the framework of general relativity, the infamous singularity, a region of infinite spacetime curvature, awaits. The tidal gravitational forces will increase dramatically as the observer approaches this point. The gravitational gradient grows, and the observer is stretched into a long, thin noodle-like structure – spaghettification, as it is so colorfully called. Every atom within his body, every particle that makes up his physical being, experiences a unique, and ultimately destructive, force. Now, let’s not forget though that this is what would happen when he sees it for himself. As he experiences an entirely different world, this observer is no longer the same observer we started with.

Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? The problem isn't necessarily the inherent complexity; rather, it stems from trying to "intuit" something that simply isn't designed to be intuited. Einstein, for all his brilliance, was fundamentally uncomfortable with the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. He famously quipped that “God does not play dice,” which I believe also explains why he missed the opportunities to study other, more promising approaches when it came to the universe. The uncertainty arises from how the universe operates at a quantum level, the probabilities are the best we can do. The problem is not that we haven't accumulated enough knowledge to "fill in the gaps." Rather, it is that there are no gaps to fill. The situation, at its best, is fundamentally probabilistic. Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? No, not in the strict sense. Antimatter, while capable of interacting with light, does not present itself as "visible matter" in the way we typically understand it. Think about it this way: "Visible matter" is, by and large, what our eyes (and other detectors) perceive. And what do they perceive? Primarily, the interaction of photons, particles of light, with atoms. When light hits matter, it can be absorbed, reflected, or transmitted. What happens depends on the properties of that matter, which, in turn, are determined by its constituent particles, their charges, their masses, and their interactions. Antimatter, on the other hand, is essentially "mirror matter." It has the same mass as normal matter, but the opposite charge. When antimatter and matter meet, they annihilate, producing energy in the form of photons. This is why antimatter can interact with light: A positron, the antimatter counterpart of the electron, for instance, can interact with photons in a variety of ways. It can absorb photons. It can scatter photons. It can emit them, too. But antimatter, in itself, is not "visible" in the same way that a rock or a tree is. A rock, when illuminated, reflects light, and the light that reflects carries with it the colors and the details we see. Antimatter does not scatter light in the same way. Instead, when antimatter encounters matter, the resulting annihilation produces a burst of energetic photons, a flash. This flash is visible, yes, but it is not really the antimatter itself that we are seeing. It is the energy released, the aftermath of the annihilation, the "explosion," if you will. If a human somehow managed to travel to the Sagittarius A* black hole, would they see exactly what the 2022 image shows us? The short answer is: Probably not. The images, after all, are based on observations made by sophisticated instruments that are, in effect, extremely sensitive radio telescopes. While, in principle, a human could travel to the vicinity of Sagittarius A*, their experience would be vastly different from what those radio telescopes record. For instance, the human would not see anything resembling a photograph. Instead, they would likely perish long before being able to send back any visually coherent data. Let's consider some of the key differences. First off, the 2022 image, which is a composite of several observations, is constructed from radio waves. Your eyes, however, are only sensitive to visible light, a very limited range of the electromagnetic spectrum. Even if your eyes could somehow adapt to radio waves, the radio waves aren't alone; gamma rays, X-rays, and other types of radiation will be far more prevalent near the black hole. The second thing is gravitational lensing. Because the gravitational field near Sagittarius A* is incredibly strong, light, any light, gets bent. So if you try to make an image of the black hole, you are going to get a distorted view. And the closer you get, the more distorted that view will become. Furthermore, as you get closer, time dilation effects will become extreme. This would necessitate taking precautions if you wanted what you observed to be consistent and, well, useful. Lastly, there is the unavoidable technical aspect of survival. The extreme tidal forces, the incredible heat, and the surrounding radiation are likely to quickly vaporize your body. So the "image" you’d get is not worth considering compared to the issues about survival and detection. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Dear Viktor Toth, with respect to your answer on the expression of the weak force, could you please correct the second equation? The first one for V(r) is right, but the second seems to have a typo, so that it is not displayed. Thank you for bringing this to my attention. I appreciate the feedback and the keen eye for detail. It appears there was indeed an error in the typesetting of the equation. My apologies for the inconvenience this may have caused. I have gone back and carefully reviewed the material in question: the expression for the potential V(r), and believe I have identified the source of confusion. The revised equation is:   V(r) = -g² * (e^(-m_W * r))/ (4 * pi * r)This expression describes the potential between two particles mediated by the massive vector bosons of the weak force. The term *g* represents the weak (coupling) charge, *m_W* denotes the mass of the W and Z bosons, and *r* is the distance between the interacting particles. This equation, as I'm sure you realize, is a consequence of the Yukawa potential, modified by the influence of the Higgs field through the mass term. In the Standard Model, the weak force acts through the exchange of these W and Z bosons, which are responsible for mediating the interactions that govern the processes such as radioactive decay, where one particle is transformed into another particle. I have now double-checked the expression to ensure accuracy. I have no problem with the notation, so feel free to ask for more clarifications if necessary, or to critique any other of my explanations on the subject. Hopefully, this addresses your concern. How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? The constancy of the speed of light is a cornerstone of the theory of relativity, and it is, at first blush, profoundly counterintuitive. After all, if time slows down, as it does in the presence of a strong gravitational field, wouldn’t that result in light’s speed being affected? The answer, unsurprisingly, is quite complex. The core idea is that the speed of light isn’t just a “speed” in the conventional sense. It isn't the kind of speed we measure for a car on a highway, for example. Instead, it’s a fundamental constant that dictates the relationship between space and time. Remember that there’s more to it than meets the eye. Both space and time are intertwined in a way we do not usually experience. If we measure the time it takes for light to travel a certain distance, the units of that distance and the unit of time being related to make the speed of light constant. The "slowing down" of time in a strong gravitational field means that the distance light covers is also “scaled” proportionally. Or, in other words, the unit of distance also changes in a similar way as the rate of time does. Thus, even though clocks tick slower in a gravitational field, the speed of light remains constant as measured locally. It’s analogous to a rubber sheet stretched out, which represents the spacetime continuum. A massive object, like a star, creates a curvature in this sheet. Now, imagine the light's trajectory can be the “shortest” path that goes along the curvature. So the light takes a longer path to traverse a greater distance. But at the same time clocks are ticking slower along this longer path. Now, in an environment with no gravity, clocks tick faster, as light travels in a more direct, straight line in shorter time intervals, light simply appears to move faster as well. However, in both situations, the measurement of the speed of light, locally, remains constant. The key is to always keep in mind how we measure time and distance. What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Let me begin by admitting that the term “tensor” sounds intimidating. It conjures images of complex notation, baffling equations, and impenetrable mathematical concepts. And while it is true that tensor calculus is a sophisticated branch of mathematics, the basic idea behind a tensor is surprisingly straightforward. Think of a tensor as just a generalization of a vector. A vector, in its simplest form, is a quantity having both magnitude and direction, such as the velocity of a moving object. But a vector is a very special kind of quantity. In particular, a vector requires a coordinate system to define it. Now, what does it mean? Imagine that you have a vector, say, the velocity of a particle, given as components in one coordinate system. If we switch to a different coordinate system, the components of the vector change. But the vector itself? Its magnitude and direction remain the same. A tensor is a mathematical object that describes a physical property that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. In other words, it is coordinate-independent. The components of a tensor change when we switch to a different coordinate system, of course, but the tensor itself, the physical property it describes remains invariant. For example, one kind of tensor describes the stress within a solid material. This stress tensor has different components depending on our coordinate system, but the actual stresses in the material are the same, regardless of the coordinate system we use to describe them. It’s the same with electricity and magnetism. Electric fields are electric fields. Magnetic fields are magnetic fields. But their behavior depends on how we orient the “coordinates” of our motion. It is the same with space-time, where the geometry of spacetime itself can be described using a tensor. But let me offer a cautionary note: Tensors are not magic. A tensor is not a thing in itself, but just a convenient mathematical structure that physicists have invented to make sure that everything “works” no matter what coordinate system (or, sometimes, even reference frame!) we choose to use. Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? The notion of “destroying” a black hole is, at best, a bit of a tricky proposition. I mean, what does it even mean to “destroy” something? Does it mean to convert it into something else? To rip it apart? To make it evaporate? The last of these options is the closest that general relativity comes to predicting some form of “black hole destruction.” However, this prediction, courtesy of Stephen Hawking, is rather… peculiar. According to Hawking, black holes are not entirely black, at least not from a theoretical perspective. Given enough time, they slowly “evaporate,” releasing their mass in the form of thermal radiation. The math is sound, but the implications are… well, they’re mind-bending, to say the least. Because a black hole’s gravitational field is so strong, it’s nearly impossible to visualize the physical process by which this radiation is created. The process is inherently a quantum phenomenon. However, given that the Hawking effect arises from a blend of general relativity and quantum mechanics, it can be said that it’s the closest thing we have to a definitive answer regarding what might be thought of as a black hole "destruction" mechanism. Still, this is a slow, slow process. For a black hole of solar mass or more, the amount of time required for this “evaporation” is unimaginably long. Certainly too long for any practical purpose. But what about other methods? Could we somehow rip a black hole apart? Could we utilize some sort of antimatter weapon, for instance? Well, there’s the problem. If a black hole has formed, it is incredibly stable, and its internal structure is, generally speaking, impossible to probe. The event horizon prevents any information from escaping. Therefore, whatever goes in the singularity, stays in the singularity. And what about the gravitational field? Indeed, the field will be strong, but not in a way that could immediately prevent someone from "escaping" if they are far far enough away (i.e., not falling in). The intense gravity is, of course, what makes a black hole so hard to "deal with." However, it is the same gravity that prevents anything from escaping once inside the event horizon. So, while a black hole’s singularity may be an inevitable consequence of its existence, the gravity is not what “destroys” anything. It just makes it, well, a black hole. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? To answer that questions, let's first reiterate the gist of that experiment. Imagine a source of light, a screen with two slits, and a detector. When light waves pass through the slits, they diffract and create an interference pattern on the detector screen. This pattern indicates wave-like behavior. Now, replace the light source with a stream of particles, and you’d expect two bright lines on the detector, corresponding to the two slits. However, strangely, when you shine light through the slits, you obtain the interference pattern: a wave-like behavior. If you block one of the slits, though, the interference pattern disappears, and you get a single bright line, as you would expect from the particles traveling through one slit. So what changes in the experiment? It's the presence or absence of observation. The observation in the double-slit experiment is not about "seeing" the light. It's about monitoring which slit the photon goes through. The experiment proves that merely knowing the path of the photon, even without “seeing” it, changes the outcome. If you attempt to determine which slit the photon passed through, the interference pattern vanishes: wave-like behavior is suppressed. The light behaves as particles. Conversely, if one doesn’t care and “doesn’t look” which slit the photons go through, the interference pattern emerges: wave-like behavior arises. This suggests that the photons are somehow passing through both slits simultaneously, creating an interference pattern. So to answer your follow up question: the visual observation determines whether the light acts as a wave or as a particle, but it matters if the light *could* interact with the observer. It's not about the act of “looking;” rather, it’s about the question of “which path.” I find it useful to think about it as a form of interaction. Any interaction breaks the interference pattern, no matter whether that interaction is something that produces visible results to me or not, and for all I know, that happens for animals I cannot observe. Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? No, it is not a coincidence. The Standard Model, while a rather complex beast, is built around a few fundamental principles. One of them is that all fundamental particles, as in, particles that do not consist of more fundamental particles, start their lives with no mass whatsoever until they interact with the Higgs field. Some do, some don’t. Neutrinos are the only known particles that, according to our current understanding, have mass but do *not* carry electric charge. Everything else does: electrons, quarks (the building blocks of protons and neutrons), and also the very mediators of the weak force, the W and Z bosons. The mechanism behind this is not that simple. So let me try a different tack. The interaction with the Higgs field is not the *only* thing that contributes to making a particle massive. By the time a proton has acquired most of its mass, only a tiny fraction of that is due to the mass of its constituent quarks and (separately) the interaction with the Higgs field. The lion's share of the proton’s mass comes from the *kinetic* energy and the *potential* energy of the gluons, the binding-force carriers that glue the quarks together inside the proton. In the case of electrons, for instance, their mass is almost 100% due to their interaction with the Higgs field. For quarks, on the other hand, it may be only about 1% of their mass. However, that does not imply that there is no relationship between charge and Higgs-field interaction; it would be incorrect to assume that. For one, quarks have mass, and as I explained, mass is related to their interaction with the Higgs field. Furthermore, the electric charge of a quark is related to how strongly it interacts with the Higgs field. The theory has been tested over and over again, and not once did it fail. Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? The Dirac equation, you see, describes relativistic spin-½ particles. It’s elegant, it's profound, and it’s crucial to understanding the quantum world. Its solutions, however, are a touch… peculiar. They predict, in addition to the “positive energy” solutions (which correspond to the particles we observe), a set of “negative energy” solutions. Now, these negative-energy solutions presented physicists with an immediate conundrum. Because energy, as we understand it, can’t be negative. It seemed to imply that the "vacuum," as it were, wasn’t empty; that an infinite sea of negative-energy particles must exist everywhere. This directly contradicted observations, and so, physicists had to come up with a better explanation. The initial attempts, as one might expect, were… rather crude. One might suggest that those negative energy solutions represent “virtual particles.” But virtual particles manifest only *inside* the calculations of quantum mechanics. Virtual particles are only an integral part of the interaction of real particles, mediating forces and ensuring the consistency of the calculations. They are not real particles themselves, at least not in the same way as the particles that comprise the world around us. It wouldn’t make sense, then, to equate the negative energy solutions to virtual matter, which, by definition, can't be directly observed or measured. The correct interpretation, the one that ultimately prevailed, was far more elegant, and it came, of course, from Dirac himself. Instead of trying to make these solutions fit into the framework of the known, Dirac proposed a radical idea: The vacuum is not truly empty. It is filled with these negative-energy states, a “sea” of particles. And, if we give that “sea” a little nudge, we might just see a vacancy (a hole) in that negative-energy “sea,” representing a particle of the opposite charge. Essentially, the negative energy solutions represent not virtual matter, but antimatter: particles with the same mass but opposite charge as their ordinary matter counterparts. And, as experiments proved in spades, that’s exactly what we observe. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? Let's start with a reality check: In 3+1 dimensions, there's one dimension of time and three dimensions of space. Since time is, in a sense, a “different beast” than space, one might ask: Does it matter what the "sign" of the time coordinate is? Does it matter that we have a “handedness” in space? The answers are interesting. First off, as far as we know, all physical laws are invariant under time reversal. What this means is that, in the Standard Model, if we were to reverse the direction of time, nothing would change, at least not in principle. We can, in other words, run all the equations backward. In the real world, however, reversing the arrow of time is something we can do only in a theoretical sense. If you “reverse time” in a real experiment, you will invariably make the system go back to square one, i.e., before the experiment started. Now, you can reverse the arrow of time if you are the Universe itself. But of course, that's not helpful. The situation with the spatial “handedness” turns out to be much more subtle. To begin with, our Universe does have a preferred, well-defined handedness. This is established by the so-called weak interaction, responsible for, among other things, radioactivity. The weak interaction differentiates between left-handed and right-handed neutrinos (and anti-neutrinos). So what happens if our "hand rule" is the opposite of nature's hand rule? The simple answer is that everything we experience would be “mirrored.” What would happen to us? As far as physics goes, it’s a non-problem. We would not be able to tell the difference. Our right hands would look like our left hands, but since the rest of the universe is doing the same, how could we know? The situation becomes trickier if we ask ourselves what happens when we start considering cosmological scales, i.e., very old light from very far away. When we look far enough, we see that the universe is not quite the same everywhere. And while the differences are subtle, there are more of one kind of galaxy than another. The explanation that we can currently offer is that the laws of physics are the same everywhere, but the initial conditions of the early universe need not be. So, it’s not as if there is a preferred “handedness” in the Universe. It’s simply that one kind of stuff out-prevailed the other. And that’s that. When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? The answer is, well… it depends on what you mean by "observe." In the conventional Copenhagen interpretation, yes, the wave function "collapses," but the term is misleading. What happens is not that the particle's state instantaneously shrinks to a point, but rather that the probabilistic description of the particle—the wave function—instantaneously changes to reflect the new information gained from the measurement. This doesn’t imply the particle was ever localized in the first place. Think of it like this: before the measurement, we might say we had a wave function that was spread out, suggesting several possible locations for the particle. After the measurement, we have a new wave function, one that is now compatible with the result of that observation. So, while the particle's description changes dramatically, the particle itself doesn't necessarily "shrink" to a smaller size, nor does it become a "packet" of any kind. The wave function is not a physical "thing" but a description of the system's state. The issue is, in our macroscopic world, we tend to think about where things are, but on quantum scales, it’s the probabilities that matter. Think of a coin toss: before you flip it, you cannot say for certain whether it will land on heads or tails. What you can say is there is a 50% chance for either. The same applies to quantum mechanics. We can only predict probabilities. What's interesting, though, is that this "collapse" isn’t some instantaneous “thing” that happens when we make the measurement. Rather, it is a reflection of our new knowledge. It’s our understanding of the system and its state that changes.

Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? The notion of an “electron” in quantum mechanics is, like the photon, a bit of a misnomer. It’s easy to fall into the trap of picturing these things as miniature billiard balls, constantly moving, occupying a well-defined location in spacetime. But an electron, just like a photon, is much better described as a probability wave that – at the moment of observation – manifests itself as a “particle” with definite properties. In other words, the electron doesn't “have” definite properties until a measurement is made. Then it “collapses”, and all the possible states of the electron – the probability waves, if you will – are suddenly reduced to a single outcome. An extremely useful – though by no means complete – analogy is this: imagine you have a shuffled deck of cards, face down. Each card, before you turn it over, can be any of the 52 cards. In a sense, all the possibilities are there, existing in a “superposition”. But once you turn the top card over, the superposition collapses. You are left with a single, definite card. While there is no physical wave associated with the electron, it is more precise (and more descriptive) to think of an electron as a probability distribution across spacetime, a distribution which – again – collapses at the moment of measurement. This is, of course, just a model. Don’t take it literally. Otherwise, you will fall victim of trying to intuit the unintuitive, which is a fool's errand. Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? First off, let me say this: The word “contradiction” is loaded. It is best to avoid it when discussing complex theoretical frameworks. Rather, one should ask: Are there any points of incompatibility? In the case of classical determinism and quantum mechanics, the answer is yes. Classical determinism posits that, given the complete specification of a system’s state at some initial time, one can, in principle, predict the future state of that system with arbitrary precision. In other words, the laws of classical physics are time-symmetric; going forwards or backward in time is equally legitimate. Quantum mechanics, by contrast, is built on the notion of probability. The time evolution of some quantum systems is captured by the Schrödinger equation that is entirely deterministic, meaning that given a certain starting state, the future state is uniquely determined. However, when we attempt to *measure* the system, its behavior is determined by probabilities. For this reason, quantum mechanics offers an intrinsic limitation on the ability to predict the precise future state of a system. This intrinsic limitation implies that the observer has no ability to predict the outcome with certainty. To be fair, one may argue that the observer is not, in any reasonable sense, part of the system. So, in principle, it might be possible to describe a system whose time evolution is deterministic and that the probabilistic behavior is caused by the interaction between the system and the observer. However, according to the well-established and empirically verified axioms of quantum mechanics, this is, *in principle*, impossible. More precisely, the system and the observer are, in practice, entangled. The interaction between them is probabilistic, and no measurement can be predicted with absolute certainty. Is that a contradiction? Arguably, yes. But, again, that’s a loaded word. What is more accurate is to say that quantum mechanics and classical determinism are incompatible. Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? No, I wouldn’t necessarily phrase it that way. My explanation of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) with the aid of “pops on a square” isn’t about “substantiating” the Olbers paradox. The Olbers paradox argues that if the universe is infinite, static, and uniformly filled with stars, then any line of sight from any observer should eventually intersect with a star. That, in turn, would mean that the entire sky should be as bright as the surface of a star. Obviously, this isn’t what we see; the sky is dark at night. The common resolution argues that the universe isn’t infinitely old; light from distant stars hasn’t had time to reach us. But there's a wrinkle. The farther away, the greater the redshift, which means that light from distant stars is, well, redshifted; shifted into the infrared and even radio bands where it is harder to see. My explanation of the CMB, though, addresses a seemingly different issue, namely the question of why the CMB spectrum is so incredibly uniform. The “pops on a square” analogy is designed to illustrate how a system can start from a state of essentially nothingness, with a highly uniform distribution of energy, and then produce a very uniform distribution later on. It’s a visual aid to grasp the concept of inflation and how it contributes to the uniformity we observe in the CMB. So does this relate to Olbers? In a way, yes. The Olbers paradox makes assumptions about the nature of our cosmological environment. The CMB, along with the understanding of inflation, provides essential information about this environment. It allows us to, for example, say something about the age of the universe, which is indeed the first step in “resolving” Olbers. Not in a direct way, though. Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately? MOND, or Modified Newtonian Dynamics, offers an alternative to the dark matter hypothesis. Instead of positing the existence of unseen matter to explain observed galactic rotation curves, MOND proposes that Newtonian gravity breaks down at extremely low accelerations. This is an “interesting” idea, and one that I spent a bit of time entertaining. But is MOND “correct”? Well, there is a mathematical formula associated with MOND. The question is: Does it reflect reality? The main challenge with MOND is that it fails in its attempts to explain gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that’s both observed and well-understood thanks to general relativity. If MOND did account for gravitational lensing, it would have to be something of a fluke, as it doesn’t come about “naturally” in MOND’s rather simplistic mathematical framework. Even more problematically, MOND struggles with the observed cosmic microwave background (the afterglow of the Big Bang). Since MOND is really a modified gravity theory, it has nothing to say about the origin of the early universe. General relativity, on the other hand, has a lot to say about the early universe, including its fluctuations, and those fluctuations turn out to be in excellent agreement with what we observe in the CMB. So MOND, while elegant, clearly suffers from significant theoretical weaknesses. Then again, neither is the dark matter hypothesis without its problems. Specifically, the observed distribution of dark matter does not match the results of computer simulations of the cosmos. Dark matter, which is posited to exist, for instance, in a giant halo surrounding our galaxy, clearly behaves differently in the simulations than it does in reality. Then there is the issue of alternatives to dark matter. Many people are working on them, and many others will undoubtedly follow. In the end, the success of a particular “answer” will depend on three things. First, does it explain all observations with a handful of free parameters? Secondly, is the theory consistent with relativity? Third, where does the theory work, what does it predict and what are its testable consequences? What would it look like to see a planet go through a wormhole as an observer? Let's first consider what comprises a wormhole. We are talking about a very distorted region of spacetime. Imagine something like a rapidly rotating black hole. From a distance, it looks like a point in space. Closer by, the intense gravity warps space. So what happens when you get close enough to the event horizon is hard to say. The observer is probably going to be torn to bits by tidal forces long before anything interesting happens. Then there's the question of what’s on the other side. If wormholes even exist, they might behave very differently from what you’d expect. What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? Mass, like the proverbial elephant in the room, is a concept that seems simple enough until you start digging. The more inertia something has, the harder it is to get it moving (or for that manner, to change its motion). The inertial mass, then, is the measure of this inertia, and in this sense, it’s a measure of how difficult it is to change an object’s velocity, or how much force is needed to change its acceleration. Next comes gravitational mass. This determines how much a gravitational force acts upon an object. An object with a large gravitational mass will experience a greater force due to a gravitational field. These two concepts may seem distinct, yet they're intricately linked together by Einstein's principle of equivalence. This principle, fundamental to general relativity, posits that inertial and gravitational masses are, in fact, the same. It's not just a convenient coincidence; it's a cornerstone of how gravity works. Then, we have rest mass, which is the mass of an object when it is at rest. It's a fundamental property of any object with mass at rest, a value that remains constant, regardless of its motion (within the realm of Newtonian physics, that is). Finally, let’s discuss variable mass. This concept actually isn’t quite as straightforward as the others in classical mechanics, because the mass doesn't change. However, in relativistic physics, especially when dealing with energy transfer, the effective mass of a system can change. The key here is the equivalence of mass and energy. Add energy to a system, and you effectively add to its mass. In our equation, f=ma, the *m* really stands for something more fundamental: inertial mass. A measurement of how much a force, *f*, will change an object’s trajectory. In most everyday experiences, we don’t need to worry about distinctions between rest mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass. However, we need to be aware of the assumptions we are making when we use the formula to solve problems. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon? It's a straightforward question, really. Photons, being massless, travel at the speed of light. The electron, on the other hand, has a non-zero rest mass. Now, a free electron (an electron not bound to an atom or anything else) doesn't have a "preferred" frame of reference. Any such electron represents a perfectly valid inertial reference frame. To fully absorb a photon, the electron would have to, in effect, "stop". However, due to the conservation of energy and momentum laws, this is impossible. Imagine a scenario: A photon, zipping along, encounters a free electron. The photon vanishes – fully absorbed – only to be replaced by a stationary electron. Where did the momentum go? The photon had momentum. Our stationary electron has no momentum. Something is amiss. In physics, you can't simply make momentum disappear. Furthermore, consider the energy. The photon had energy (E=hf, with f denoting its frequency, a measure of its energy). If the electron is now standing still, where is the energy going? It has to go somewhere; energy isn't lost in the process due to the law of energy conservation. Now, let's examine what really happens when a photon encounters a free electron. The electron interacts with the photon, absorbs some energy and momentum, becoming a “scattered” electron. The only way the interaction can proceed is by the electron scattering, i.e., changing its direction of motion and absorbing some of the photon's energy and momentum in the process. This way, both energy and momentum are conserved. The electron may increase its velocity but never comes to a complete stop. Also, the initial photon will also be gone. Instead, it will transform with another, lower-energy, photon to preserve energy. This is the process of Compton scattering. I’m not saying that a free electron is incapable of absorbing a photon’s energy. It can. I'm just pointing out that it can’t fully absorb a photon and come to rest or "disappear" in the process. The act of a "photon being absorbed" can only occur when and if the electron "wants" to. This may seem odd but photons and electrons' fate is tied due to their interaction with one another. It is the core temperature and the amount of fuel that matter more than any of the aforementioned general relativistic effects. You see, although for all practical purposes, stars are born in the same way regardless of which theory of gravity we use, that is not to say that general relativity is not important. Far from it. How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? The Standard Model of particle physics posits that quarks are fundamental particles with a nonzero mass. These masses, however, only account for about 1% of the proton's mass and about 1.5% of the neutron's mass. So, if the quarks themselves are so comparatively light, where does the rest of the mass come from? The answer lies in the strong force, a force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. Because of the nature of the strong force, quarks cannot exist in isolation, a phenomenon known as color confinement. When we try to pull quarks apart, the potential energy between them increases linearly with the distance. This is because, unlike electromagnetism or gravity, the strong force does not diminish with distance. Instead, the force grows stronger. Eventually, the energy stored in the field between the quarks becomes so large that it overcomes the mass-energy relationship, resulting in the creation of a quark-antiquark pair. This pair materializes, "canceling" the stress in the field and forming new composite particles, such as mesons. But it is the force-carrying particles of the strong force, called gluons, that play a crucial role in determining the mass of a proton or neutron. These gluons mediate the strong interaction between quarks and, like the photons of electromagnetism, are massless. However, gluons also interact with each other, a property that results in an extremely powerful attractive force, leading to an environment of sorts that makes the masses of these particles. The exact computation relies on both the mass of the individual quarks and the interplay between the kinetic energy of the quarks and the energy stored in the gluon fields. So, in the end, the mass of a proton or neutron is a combination of the masses and momenta of the constituent quarks plus the energy of the gluons that are constantly exchanged between them. This energy manifests as a huge quantity of invariant mass--a far cry from the individual masses of the quarks themselves, making the gluons critical to the mass of the bound state. How does a black hole destroy matter but not light? Why is it that light can escape, or at least, propagate away from a black hole, while matter is doomed to get pulled in? The answer, as with many things in physics, lies in the specifics: in the interactions. Matter, as we know it, consists of particles that are either massive, or have rest mass. Mass is coupled to gravity, and also couples to other forces (electromagnetism, weak force, strong force) that mediate interactions with other matter. Well, gravity is very strong, but the black hole does not directly “suck in” everything. Instead, what happens is that objects are pulled toward the black hole. The trajectory of these objects change over time, and unless they are moving away from the black hole at a sufficient speed, they eventually end up inside the event horizon. Light, however, is different. Light is comprised of photons, which have zero rest mass. They are also not charged, so they do not interact via the electromagnetic force. The key is that massless particles, like the photon, follow null geodesics: the shortest path through spacetime, which is described by the geometry of spacetime. And while a black hole's gravity influences the path of any particle, including the photon, the photon itself is not “pulled in” the way that, say, a massive object is. Instead, the photon's trajectory curves. However, if the photon ventures too close to the black hole, its path towards the far field becomes altered such that it is curved back, toward the black hole. No surprise: this is precisely what happens when the photon passes within the event horizon; it cannot escape. But, a photon that is a good distance from the black hole can escape. The photons, despite the very strong gravity, are not destroyed; they merely travel in different directions. Contrast this with a massive particle, which, once past the event horizon, cannot avoid encountering the inevitable singularity at the center of the black hole. How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? Let me start by pointing out that the term “virtual particle” is not meant to describe something “less real”. This is another one of those expressions that do more harm than good, and a source of considerable confusion, in fact. Reality is, in itself, a rather complicated business. We know that the world is not deterministic. The best we can do regarding the outcomes of our observations is to predict probabilities. So what does it mean for something to be “real”? It implies that probability is close to 1. But any particle has a certain probability of being detected, and yes, there are also probabilities linked to so-called “virtual particles,” too. To understand the distinction, it might be helpful to consider the concept of Feynman diagrams, a crucial set of tools for particle physicists. When we calculate the probability of, say, an electron scattering off another electron, we don’t picture an interaction in which those two charged particles simply meet, deflect each other, and go their separate ways. Rather, we calculate the probability of the electron emitting a photon and then, well, absorbing it. That emitted photon is often thought of as a “virtual photon.” Why virtual? Because the amount of energy and momentum it carries are not consistent with the usual relationship between energy, momentum, and mass. Can such a “virtual photon” ever exist on its own, as a real photon? The answer is no because of fundamental conservation laws. Likewise, a virtual electron can only come into existence (and then immediately vanishes) in the presence of some other charged particle. As the word “virtual” suggests, the virtual particle is an intermediary, never being observed directly. But then, how does Hawking radiation do it? Well, the key is to understand the difference between “empty space” in our everyday intuition and “empty space” in the quantum field theory. In quantum field theory, “empty space” is not empty; it is filled with fields. Fields that can fluctuate. In the presence of a black hole, the gravitational field is very strong. At the so-called event horizon, those fields can fluctuate enormously, so much so that a “virtual particle pair,” a particle and antiparticle, for instance, an electron and positron, might spontaneously and quickly appear very briefly (as required by Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle). Then, one of these particles may cross the event horizon, gets swallowed by the black hole, never to be seen again. The other one escapes, appearing as “real” Hawking radiation. Note that the total energy of the particle and the antiparticle is zero. The black hole in effect supplies the energy to change this zero-energy “virtual particle” into “real” radiation.

Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? Hawking radiation is a fascinating prediction of physics, and it does raise the eyebrows of many. What would happen if something went through a black hole? The most straightforward answer leans towards invoking the concept of the equivalence principle. You see, an object falling into a black hole is, in principle, no different from an object accelerating in an elevator. The equivalence principle posits that gravity is, in essence, indistinguishable from acceleration. That, by itself, is not quite good enough, though. The problem with a black hole is that the gravitational field increases without bound as you approach the singularity. So, you're also dealing with tidal forces, which are the result of the difference in gravitational force across the extent of your body. If you fall feet first, your feet will experience a much stronger gravitational force than your head. As a result, you will be stretched out, or spaghettified, if you will. Now, assuming that whatever you are made of can withstand this stretching (which it can't, of course, but let's play along with the thought experiment), what will happen? Well, beyond the event horizon, there is no way the object will ever reach a location outside. Not in any finite amount of time, anyway, as measured by any observer outside the event horizon. So the object "falls". And as far as it is concerned, it keeps falling. Now, what appears to be falling for an external observer? Well, a static picture. The object appears to slow down, becoming redshifted, dimmer, and eventually invisible. In reality, what the object's internal clock will measure is a certain amount of elapsed time. But from the point of view of an external observer, the object will essentially freeze at the event horizon. The only thing that will change is that the black hole has more mass (and probably more angular momentum if the infalling object had any). The event horizon also changes slightly, becoming just a tad larger. But there is nothing *that* interesting taking place for the external observer.
